title: General Principles of Law, Unilateral Acts and Subsidiary Means

slides.title: Article 38 once more — now for (c) and (d)
slides.text: The catalogue is quoted a third time because this lecture covers what is left after treaties and custom: subparagraph (c), the general principles of law, and subparagraph (d), judicial decisions and teachings as subsidiary means. Unilateral acts, which the lecture also covers, appear nowhere in Article 38 at all.

slides.title: The ILC's work on general principles
slides.text: The International Law Commission took up general principles in 2019 with Special Rapporteur Marcelo Vázquez-Bermúdez. The second report of 2021 set out the structure now generally used: general principles come in two kinds — those DERIVED FROM NATIONAL LEGAL SYSTEMS, which require a principle common to the principal legal systems of the world plus its transposition to the international legal system, and those FORMED WITHIN the international legal system itself. That two-track division is what to carry away from this slide.

cards.q: According to the ILC's work, what are the two kinds of general principles of law?
cards.a: Those derived from national legal systems — requiring a principle common to the principal legal systems of the world plus transposition to the international level — and those formed within the international legal system itself.

slides.title: What general principles are and what they are for
slides.text: Unlike treaties and custom, general principles are unwritten law NOT created by the will of states — which is why they sit uneasily in a consent-based system. How they are found is contested: by the comparative approach, by comparing the principal legal systems; or, some say, by a natural-law approach. The phrase 'civilized nations' in Article 38(1)(c) is today regarded as an embarrassing relic and is read as 'the principal legal systems of the world'. Their purpose is stated in two words on the slide: gap filling — they keep a court from having to declare a non liquet when neither treaty nor custom answers the question.

terms.def: Identifying a general principle by showing it is common to the principal legal systems of the world.
A declaration that the law provides no answer; general principles exist largely to prevent one.

cards.q: What function do general principles of law serve in the system of sources?
cards.a: Gap filling: they supply a rule where neither treaty nor custom answers, so a court need not declare a non liquet. Unlike the other sources they are not created by the will of states.

cards.q: How is the phrase 'recognized by civilized nations' in Article 38(1)(c) understood today?
cards.a: As a dated formulation to be read as 'the principal legal systems of the world'; the wording survives in the Statute but carries no normative weight of its own.

slides.title: General principles in an arbitration clause
slides.text: Article V of the Claims Settlement Declaration of Algiers of 19 January 1981, which created the Iran-United States Claims Tribunal, directs the tribunal to decide all cases on the basis of respect for law, applying such choice of law rules and principles of commercial and international law as it determines to be applicable, taking account of usages of trade, contract provisions and changed circumstances. It is an example of parties writing general principles into the applicable law of a dispute settlement mechanism.

slides.title: General principles in EU law
slides.text: Two Treaty provisions show the technique used inside a legal order. Article 340(2) TFEU makes the Union liable in non-contractual matters in accordance with the general principles common to the laws of the Member States — the comparative method written into a treaty. Article 6(3) TEU provides that fundamental rights, as guaranteed by the ECHR and as they result from the constitutional traditions common to the Member States, constitute general principles of Union law. Both will come back in the EU half of the exam.

terms.def: Non-contractual liability of the Union, determined by the general principles common to the laws of the Member States.
Fundamental rights from the ECHR and from common constitutional traditions are general principles of Union law.

cards.q: Which two EU Treaty provisions use the technique of general principles, and for what?
cards.a: Art 340(2) TFEU for the non-contractual liability of the Union, by reference to principles common to the laws of the Member States; and Art 6(3) TEU, making fundamental rights from the ECHR and common constitutional traditions general principles of Union law.

slides.title: Internationale Handelsgesellschaft
slides.text: Case 11/70: respect for fundamental rights forms an integral part of the general principles of law protected by the Court of Justice; that protection, while inspired by the constitutional traditions common to the Member States, must be ensured within the framework of the structure and objectives of the Community. Two things at once — the Court accepts fundamental rights as a source of review, but insists on defining them autonomously rather than importing national constitutions. That reservation is what makes the case a landmark in the EU half of the course too.

cards.q: What did Internationale Handelsgesellschaft establish about fundamental rights in the EU legal order?
cards.a: That respect for fundamental rights is an integral part of the general principles of law protected by the Court of Justice — inspired by common constitutional traditions, but ensured autonomously within the framework and objectives of the Community.

slides.title: The catalogue of general principles
slides.text: The working list: venire contra factum proprium, i.e. estoppel; compensation for causing harm; unjust enrichment; interest for late payment; responsibility for unlawful behaviour; state of necessity; and abuse of rights. Notice what they have in common — they are all principles a private lawyer would recognise, which is exactly the comparative origin the ILC describes. The slides that follow give an authority for several of them.

terms.def: No one may contradict their own previous conduct to another's detriment; the civilian expression of estoppel.
A right may not be exercised for a purpose alien to the one for which it was conferred.

cards.q: Name five general principles of law recognised in international practice.
cards.a: Estoppel (venire contra factum proprium), compensation for causing harm, unjust enrichment, interest for late payment, responsibility for unlawful behaviour, state of necessity, abuse of rights — any five.

slides.title: Estoppel: its elements
slides.text: In the Land, Island and Maritime Frontier Dispute the ICJ stated the essential elements required by estoppel: a statement or representation made by one party to another, and reliance upon it by that other party to his detriment or to the advantage of the party making it. Two elements, then — representation plus detrimental reliance. Apply them in that order in a problem question; a mere inconsistency without reliance is not estoppel.

terms.def: A party may not resile from a representation on which another has relied to its detriment, or to the maker's advantage.

cards.q: What are the two elements of estoppel in international law?
cards.a: A statement or representation made by one party to another, and reliance on it by that other party to its detriment or to the advantage of the party making it (El Salvador/Honduras, ICJ 1990).

slides.title: Force majeure: the Russian Indemnity case
slides.text: The 1912 award in the Russian Indemnity case, quoted in French, holds that the plea of force majeure is available in public international law as much as in private law, and that a state's obligation to perform treaties may yield if the very existence of the state is endangered — if performance would be self-destructive. Two lessons: general principles migrate from private law into international law, and even pacta sunt servanda has an outer limit.

terms.def: An irresistible force or unforeseen event making performance materially impossible, precluding wrongfulness.

slides.title: Necessity: ILC Article 25
slides.text: Necessity is the most tightly fenced of the principles, and the Article is best learned as a four-part filter. It may be invoked only if the act (a) is the ONLY way to safeguard an essential interest against a GRAVE and IMMINENT peril, and (b) does not seriously impair an essential interest of the other state or of the international community as a whole. And it is excluded altogether if the obligation itself rules necessity out, or if the state has CONTRIBUTED to the situation of necessity. Every one of those conditions is a place where an exam answer can show its work.

terms.def: ILC Art 25: a circumstance precluding wrongfulness where the act is the only way to safeguard an essential interest against a grave and imminent peril and does not seriously impair another's essential interest.

cards.q: State A breaches an obligation to avert an economic crisis it caused by its own policy. Can it invoke necessity?
cards.a: No. Under ILC Article 25(2)(b) necessity is excluded where the state has contributed to the situation of necessity — quite apart from the requirements that the act be the only way to safeguard an essential interest against a grave and imminent peril.

cards.q: List the conditions for invoking necessity under ILC Article 25.
cards.a: The act must be the only way to safeguard an essential interest against a grave and imminent peril, and must not seriously impair an essential interest of the obligee state or of the international community. It is excluded if the obligation rules it out or if the state contributed to the necessity.

slides.title: Unjust enrichment, found comparatively
slides.text: Inceysa Vallisoletana v. El Salvador shows the comparative method in action: the tribunal reasoned that the written legal systems of nations governed by the civil law recognise that where the cause of an increase in someone's assets is illegal, such enrichment must be sanctioned by preventing its consummation. The tribunal is not citing a treaty or custom; it is surveying domestic systems and transposing what it finds.

slides.title: General principles in administrative tribunals
slides.text: Franks and Vollering v. EPO: the law the tribunal applies to claims includes not just the written rules of the defendant organization but general principles of law and basic human rights. This is the second ILC category at work — principles formed within the international legal system, used to fill gaps in the internal law of an international organization.

slides.title: Which principles, concretely
slides.text: J.M.W. v. EPO names them: the general principles enshrined in the Convention, particularly non-discrimination and the protection of property rights, are part of human rights, which under the tribunal's case law apply to relations with staff. Together with the previous slide the message is that an international organization cannot treat its staff outside the law merely because its own rules are silent.

cards.q: Why do general principles matter for the internal law of an international organization?
cards.a: Because the organization's written rules are incomplete: tribunals hold that the applicable law includes general principles and basic human rights — non-discrimination and protection of property among them — which apply even to staff relations.

slides.title: Unilateral acts: the definition
slides.text: Acts and declarations made with the INTENTION to create, modify or end international legal rights and obligations. The slide puts an exclamation mark after 'Intention!' because that is the whole test — the same words spoken without that intention are politics, not law. Unilateral acts split into the fully unilateral, such as recognition and protest, and the partly unilateral, which operate in connection with a treaty: ratification, a reservation, a protest against a reservation.

terms.def: An act or declaration by which a state intends to create, modify or end international rights and obligations.

cards.q: What distinguishes a unilateral legal act from a political statement?
cards.a: The intention to create, modify or end international legal rights and obligations. Without that intention the same words produce no legal effect.

cards.q: Give examples of fully unilateral and partly unilateral acts.
cards.a: Fully unilateral: recognition, protest. Partly unilateral: acts connected with a treaty — ratification, a reservation, a protest against a reservation.

slides.title: Why a unilateral declaration binds
slides.text: The ILC's 2006 Guiding Principles answer the obvious objection — how can a state bind itself without an agreement? Principle 1: declarations publicly made and manifesting the will to be bound may create legal obligations; when the conditions are met the binding character rests on GOOD FAITH; other states may take them into consideration and rely on them, and are entitled to require that the obligations be respected. The basis is therefore not consent of the other side but the protection of reliance.

terms.def: Guiding Principles applicable to unilateral declarations of States capable of creating legal obligations.

cards.q: On what basis does a unilateral declaration bind the state that made it?
cards.a: Good faith. Under ILC Guiding Principle 1, a declaration publicly made and manifesting the will to be bound creates obligations because other states may rely on it and are entitled to require that it be respected.

slides.title: The four types of unilateral act
slides.text: Promise, renouncement, protest and recognition — the last of which splits into recognition in general and recognition of states or governments. Keep them apart by their direction: a promise adds an obligation for the author, a renouncement gives up a right of the author, a protest preserves the author's position against another's conduct, and recognition accepts a situation as legally valid.

terms.def: A unilateral act preserving the author's legal position and preventing acquiescence in another state's conduct.
A unilateral act giving up a right.

cards.q: Name the four types of unilateral act and what each does.
cards.a: Promise (assumes an obligation), renouncement (gives up a right), protest (preserves the author's position and prevents acquiescence), recognition (accepts a situation, or a state or government, as legally valid).

slides.title: The Ihlen Declaration
slides.text: The classic case. In 1919 the Norwegian foreign minister Ihlen told the Danish envoy that the Norwegian Government would not make difficulties over the settlement of the Greenland question. In Eastern Greenland the Permanent Court held it beyond all dispute that a reply of this nature, given by a foreign minister on behalf of his Government, in response to a request by the diplomatic representative of a foreign Power, on a question within his province, is binding upon his country. Three conditions are embedded in that sentence: the right office, acting for the government, on a matter within its competence.

terms.def: An oral statement by the Norwegian foreign minister held binding on Norway in PCIJ, Legal Status of Eastern Greenland (1933).

cards.q: Why was the Ihlen Declaration binding on Norway although it was a single oral remark?
cards.a: Because it was given by the Minister for Foreign Affairs on behalf of his Government, in response to a request by a foreign state's diplomatic representative, on a question falling within his province — PCIJ, Eastern Greenland 1933.

slides.title: How a unilateral declaration is interpreted
slides.text: Guiding Principle 7 sets a deliberately high bar and a deliberately narrow reading. A unilateral declaration entails obligations only if stated in clear and specific terms; in case of doubt about the scope, the obligations must be interpreted RESTRICTIVELY; and weight is given first and foremost to the text, together with the context and circumstances in which it was made. Contrast this with treaty interpretation under Article 31 VCLT, where no such restrictive presumption exists — the difference is that nobody gave anything in return here.

cards.q: How does interpretation of a unilateral declaration differ from interpretation of a treaty?
cards.a: A unilateral declaration binds only if stated in clear and specific terms, and in case of doubt its obligations are construed restrictively (ILC Guiding Principle 7). Article 31 VCLT contains no such restrictive presumption.

slides.title: Form is not decisive: Nuclear Tests
slides.text: In the Nuclear Tests cases the ICJ held that whether a statement is made orally or in writing makes no essential difference: statements made in particular circumstances may create commitments in international law, which does not require written form. The question of form is not decisive. Read together with the Ihlen Declaration, this is the rule that a press conference can bind a state — which is why Guiding Principle 7 then insists on clarity and restrictive interpretation.

cards.q: Must a binding unilateral declaration be in writing?
cards.a: No. Nuclear Tests: whether the statement is oral or written makes no essential difference; form is not decisive. What matters is the intention to be bound, manifested publicly and in clear terms.

slides.title: Subsidiary means: what they are
slides.text: Three groups. Decisions of international and national courts and tribunals — with the crucial caveat that Article 59 of the ICJ Statute precludes stare decisis. Teachings, meaning specialists and learned bodies such as the ILC, the Institut de Droit International and the International Law Association. And soft law: codes of conduct, standards and the like. None of them creates law; all of them help determine what the law is.

terms.def: Institut de Droit International and International Law Association — learned societies whose resolutions count among the 'teachings'.

slides.title: How much weight a subsidiary means carries
slides.text: Draft Conclusion 3 of the ILC's 2023 work gives six criteria, and they are the answer to the exam question 'how much does this authority prove?': the degree of representativeness, the quality of the reasoning, the expertise of those involved, the level of agreement among them, the reception by states and other entities, and, where applicable, the mandate conferred on the body. A unanimous ILC conclusion adopted with a General Assembly mandate and well received by states sits at the top; a single scholar's article sits far below.

cards.q: By what criteria is the weight of a subsidiary means assessed?
cards.a: Degree of representativeness, quality of the reasoning, expertise of those involved, level of agreement among them, reception by states, and the mandate conferred on the body (ILC Draft Conclusion 3, 2023).

slides.title: Article 38(1)(d) read with Article 59
slides.text: The two provisions must be read together and the lecture puts them side by side for that reason. Article 38(1)(d) admits judicial decisions and teachings as subsidiary means 'subject to the provisions of Article 59'; Article 59 then provides that the decision of the Court has no binding force except between the parties and in respect of that particular case. The second provision is what keeps the first from turning into a doctrine of precedent.

terms.def: An ICJ decision binds only the parties and only in respect of that particular case.

cards.q: How do Articles 38(1)(d) and 59 of the ICJ Statute interact?
cards.a: Article 38(1)(d) admits judicial decisions as subsidiary means, but expressly 'subject to Article 59', under which a decision binds only the parties in that case — so case law informs but never binds generally.

slides.title: What stare decisis means
slides.text: The definition from Black's Law Dictionary: the policy of courts to stand by precedent and not disturb a settled point; once a court has laid down a principle applicable to a certain state of facts, it will adhere to it and apply it to all future cases where the facts are substantially the same, regardless of whether the parties and the property are the same. This is the common-law doctrine that international law does NOT have — the slide is here so that you can say precisely what is being denied.

terms.def: The common-law doctrine of binding precedent; not part of international law.

slides.title: No precedent, but jurisprudence constante
slides.text: SGS v. Philippines states the position and its qualification in one breath: there is no doctrine of precedent in international law, if by precedent is meant a rule of the binding effect of a single decision — but it must be for the longer term, through the development of a common legal opinion or jurisprudence constante, to resolve difficult questions. In other words, a single decision binds nobody, yet a consistent line of decisions acquires real authority.

terms.def: A settled line of decisions whose authority comes from consistency rather than from any single judgment being binding.

cards.q: If there is no binding precedent in international law, why do lawyers cite earlier decisions at all?
cards.a: Because a consistent line of decisions — jurisprudence constante — develops a common legal opinion and carries real persuasive authority, even though no single decision binds anyone but the parties to it.

slides.title: The same problem in the WTO
slides.text: Japan – Taxes on Alcoholic Beverages says it for trade law: adopted panel reports are an important part of the GATT acquis, are often considered by subsequent panels, create legitimate expectations among WTO Members and should be taken into account where relevant — however, they are not binding except for resolving the particular dispute between the parties. The formula 'legitimate expectations, but not binding' is the practical middle position across all international adjudication.

terms.def: The accumulated body of decisions and practice of a regime; here the GATT/WTO case law.

slides.title: The ILC's current formulation
slides.text: Draft Conclusion 7 of 2024 closes the topic: decisions of international courts or tribunals may be followed on points of law where they address the same or similar issues, but such decisions do not constitute legally binding precedent unless otherwise provided for in a specific instrument or rule of international law. Note the escape clause at the end — a treaty can create binding precedent if the parties want it, which is why the position must always be checked against the instrument in front of you.

cards.q: State the current ILC position on precedent in international law.
cards.a: Decisions of international courts may be followed on points of law addressing the same or similar issues, but they are not legally binding precedent unless a specific instrument or rule of international law provides otherwise (Draft Conclusion 7, 2024).
